newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP rejects bid to crack down on expense claims.
newsitem.headline: EP rejects bid to crack down on expense claims.

text.p: Euro-MPs on Thursday blocked an attempt to clear up the controversy surrounding their allowances, in spite of regular claims from inside and outside the European Parliament that the system is being abused.
Euro-deputies are paid a set rate for travelling and living expenses, depending on the distance between their constituencies and the parliament's seats in Brussels and Strasbourg.
They are not obliged to produce documents to support their expense claims and can sign on in the parliament to claim their daily allowance only to walk out five minutes later.
The system has led to allegations that some Euro-MPs, who are paid by national governments at widely differing rates, have been fiddling their expenses.
"There are problems because some people compensate for having a low salary from travel expenses," a parliament official told Reuters recently.
"If we had a single statute -- and therefore a common salary scale -- it would get rid of a lot of the problems," he said.

Belgian Socialist deputy Philippe de Coene attempted on Thursday to get parliament to write into its 1998 budget report a commitment that allowances "should be payable only on the basis of costs really incurred, which must be corroborated by supporting documents".
But a majority of Euro-MPs rejected the proposal.
The move echoes a similar call made last November by the then president of parliament German Socialist Klaus Haensch.

In a letter circulated to the parliament's vice-presidents and political group leaders (the Bureau), Haensch said Euro-MPs should be obliged to produce proof of travel and said a statute for Euro-deputies must be drafted early next year.
The Bureau set up a working party in January to draw up new rules based on Haensch's recommendations but has not yet finished its work, even though it was supposed to do so in April.
Euro-MPs said they wanted the report by September. Opponents of Haensch's proposal argue that it would require too much costly administration.
The new EU treaty, clinched in Amsterdam last week, gives Euro-MPs the right to draw up a single statute for deputies from all 15 member states, but the final say still lies with EU governments.

The 1998 budget report estimates that parliament will spend nearly 18 million ecus next year on expenses from a budget of some 905 million ecus, a large chunk of which will be poured into its new buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg.
The new 40-billion-Belgian-franc hemicycle in Brussels has massively overshot its original budget.
On insistence from the French, the Amsterdam treaty obliges the assembly to hold 12 sessions in Strasbourg, instead of 11 as now -- the parliament being shut in August.
The extra session will cost European taxpayers an extra 1.866 million ecus, according to British Socialist John Tomlinson, who drew up the 1998 budget report.
The parliament's monthly travelling circus involve 1,110 auxiliary staff, 1,870 interpreters and conference technicians, 2,232 hired vehicles and 2,311 telephones, faxes and televisions.
